title: Secondary Amenorrhea: hCG First, Then FSH to Find the Break
summary: Learn the first round of tests for secondary amenorrhea, why the progestin challenge is now treated with caution, and how FSH, estradiol and age separate premature ovarian insufficiency, menopause and central causes.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 26 Hit 5 (amenorrhea workup sequence), Hit 14 (12 months amenorrhea + FSH 85 + estradiol <10) and Exam Trap 3 (FSH/LH before the progestin challenge), checked against Gibson 2020, Nelson 2023, the ESHRE 2024 POI guideline and the WHO menopause fact sheet. Open reviews measure FSH with prolactin and TSH in the first round after hCG and caution against routine progestin challenge, so the reviewer’s fixed five-step order is taught as the older approach (register flag rv-amenorrhea-fixed-sequence). Hit 14’s “primary ovarian failure (menopause)” needs age context: under 40 is POI (register flag rv-fsh-menopause-vs-poi). The STRAW+10 papers on PMC were blocked by a browser verification page and were not read. Not taught: primary amenorrhea, PCOS criteria, androgen thresholds.

objectives: State why hCG is the first test in every patient with amenorrhea and which hormones are measured in the first round.
Explain how FSH locates the lesion (ovary vs hypothalamus/pituitary) and why the progestin challenge is used with caution.
Distinguish premature ovarian insufficiency from menopause using age, duration of amenorrhea and FSH.

scenes.title: Three women, no periods
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients with secondary amenorrhea. (1) A 27-year-old, no period for 6 months, with hot flushes. (2) A 22-year-old distance runner who has lost weight, no period for 8 months. (3) A 52-year-old, no period for 12 months: FSH 85 mIU/mL, estradiol <10 pg/mL. Question token: “Which test first, and what is FSH telling you?”

cues.text: Three women have stopped having periods. A twenty-seven-year-old with hot flushes, six months without a period. A twenty-two-year-old runner who has lost weight, eight months.
And a fifty-two-year-old, twelve months without a period, with an FSH of eighty-five and an estradiol below ten.
Which test comes first for all three, and what is FSH telling you about where the problem lies?

props.label: Which test first? What is FSH telling you?

scenes.title: The axis behind a period
scenes.altText: Schematic of the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis as four stacked boxes: hypothalamus (GnRH) → anterior pituitary (FSH, LH) → ovary (estradiol, progesterone) → endometrium. Estradiol and progesterone feed back negatively on the hypothalamus and pituitary. After ovulation, the corpus luteum works for about 14 days unless rescued by hCG from an embryo; falling progesterone then triggers menses. Lesion map: central (hypothalamus or pituitary) causes give low or normal FSH; a failing ovary gives high FSH because negative feedback is lost; in one review’s table, high prolactin, PCOS and uterine (Asherman) causes sit in the low-or-normal-FSH group.

cues.text: A period is the last step of a chain. The hypothalamus releases GnRH, the pituitary answers with FSH and LH, and the ovary makes estradiol and progesterone.
Estradiol and progesterone feed back to slow the hypothalamus and pituitary. If no embryo makes hCG, the corpus luteum fades after about two weeks, progesterone falls, and the lining sheds.
So the first question is where the chain is broken: centrally, in the hypothalamus or pituitary, or peripherally, in the ovary, uterus or outflow tract.
FSH points the way. A failing ovary loses its feedback, so FSH climbs. A central cause leaves FSH low or normal.

props.title: Feedback
lines: No hCG → corpus luteum fades ~14 d

props.label: Ovary fails → FSH ↑ · central → FSH low/normal

scenes.title: The modern first round of tests
scenes.altText: Workup card: (1) exclude pregnancy with hCG in every patient, whatever the stated sexual history; (2) in the same initial round, measure FSH (with LH and estradiol), prolactin and TSH; one review adds testosterone and a pelvic ultrasound; (3) an androgen panel (total and free testosterone, androstenedione, DHEAS, 17-hydroxyprogesterone) if there are signs of androgen excess. Caution card: hormonal contraception can hide amenorrhea and lower FSH. Progestin challenge card: medroxyprogesterone acetate 5–10 mg for 5–10 days; bleeding 2–7 days after finishing is a positive test; no bleed may mean an outflow problem or low estrogen; experts caution against routine use because it may be unreliable and is associated with false-negative withdrawals; in a published case a woman with POI bled after the challenge twice.

cues.text: Step one never changes: rule out pregnancy with hCG in every patient, whatever she says about her sexual history.

Current reviews then measure FSH, with LH and estradiol, together with prolactin and TSH in the same first round. One adds testosterone and a pelvic ultrasound, and an androgen panel follows if there are signs of androgen excess.

The older progestin challenge gives five to ten milligrams of medroxyprogesterone for five to ten days. Bleeding two to seven days after the last dose is positive. No bleeding suggests an outflow problem or too little estrogen.

But experts caution against routine use: the test may be unreliable and gives false-negative results, and one published patient with ovarian insufficiency bled after it twice. Also remember that hormonal contraception can hide amenorrhea and lower FSH.

props.title: Progestin challenge
lines: No bleed: outflow or low estrogen

scenes.title: Reading FSH: POI, menopause or central
scenes.altText: Three result cards. POI (ESHRE 2024): before age 40, spontaneous amenorrhea or irregular cycles for at least 4 months plus FSH >25 IU/L; one elevated FSH is enough, repeat after 4–6 weeks only if uncertain; no need to time it to cycle day; do not diagnose from estradiol alone, but low estradiol with high FSH adds confirmation; AMH is not the primary test. Menopause (WHO): natural menopause is recognised after 12 consecutive months without menstruation with no other cause, generally between 45 and 55; ESHRE calls ovarian failure at 40–44 early menopause. Central (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea pattern): low LH and FSH with low estradiol — hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Hook answers: (1) 27-year-old: hCG, then FSH, prolactin, TSH; a high FSH would point to POI; (2) runner: hCG first; low FSH/LH with low estradiol would fit hypothalamic amenorrhea; (3) 52-year-old: 12 months, FSH 85 mIU/mL (= 85 IU/L), estradiol <10 pg/mL: menopause.

cues.text: High FSH points to a failing ovary, and age decides the label. Before forty, ESHRE’s 2024 guideline diagnoses premature ovarian insufficiency from four months of absent or irregular cycles plus one FSH above twenty-five international units per litre.
Repeat FSH after four to six weeks only if the picture is unclear. Estradiol alone does not make the diagnosis, but a low value with high FSH supports it.

Natural menopause is recognised after twelve consecutive months without a period and no other cause, usually between forty-five and fifty-five. Low FSH and LH with low estradiol instead points to a central cause, such as hypothalamic amenorrhea.

Back to the hook. All three start with hCG. The twenty-seven-year-old with a high FSH would have ovarian insufficiency, the runner’s low FSH and estradiol would fit hypothalamic amenorrhea, and the fifty-two-year-old is menopausal.

props.title: Hook answers (hCG first for all)
lines: 2 Runner, FSH and estradiol low → central

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “FSH waits until after the progestin challenge” (✓ current reviews measure FSH with prolactin and TSH in the first round after hCG); “A withdrawal bleed means the ovaries are fine” (✓ the challenge may be unreliable; a woman with POI bled after it); “High FSH + low estradiol always = menopause” (✓ age decides: under 40 is POI; natural menopause is recognised after 12 months, usually 45–55).

cues.text: Trap one: FSH must wait until after the progestin challenge. No: current reviews check FSH with prolactin and TSH in the first round, right after hCG.
Trap two: a withdrawal bleed means the ovaries are fine. No: the challenge may be unreliable, and a woman with ovarian insufficiency still bled.
Trap three: high FSH with low estradiol always means menopause. No: under forty the same pattern is premature ovarian insufficiency.

props.title: ✗ “FSH only after the progestin challenge.”
lines: ✓ FSH, prolactin, TSH in the first round

props.title: ✗ “Withdrawal bleed = ovaries fine.”
lines: ✓ May be unreliable; POI can still bleed

scenes.title: Rule out the baby, then ask who is shouting
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Rule out the baby, then ask who is shouting.” hCG first. Then FSH: a pituitary SHOUTING (high FSH) at an ovary that cannot answer means ovarian failure; a WHISPERING pituitary (low or normal FSH) means the problem is upstream. Age names the failure: under 40 POI, 12 months at the usual age menopause. Tokens: baby = hCG · shouting = high FSH · whisper = central. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: rule out the baby, then ask who is shouting. A pituitary shouting high FSH at a silent ovary means ovarian failure. A whispering pituitary means the problem is upstream.
Where it breaks: hormonal contraception can quiet FSH, causes such as high prolactin, polycystic ovary syndrome or Asherman syndrome do not raise FSH, and an uncertain FSH may need repeating.

props.text: Rule out the baby, then ask who is shouting

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Prolactin, PCOS, uterine causes: FSH not high

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “hCG first · then FSH, prolactin, TSH together · progestin challenge unreliable”, “FSH high: under 40 = POI · 12 months at usual age = menopause · FSH low = central”.

cues.text: Rule out pregnancy first, then read FSH alongside prolactin and TSH, because a high FSH points to ovarian failure, which is premature ovarian insufficiency before age 40 and menopause after twelve months without periods at the usual age.

props.label: hCG first · FSH, prolactin, TSH together · challenge unreliable
FSH ↑: < 40 = POI · 12 months at usual age = menopause · FSH ↓ = central

explanation.what: Plain language: when periods stop, first make sure the woman is not pregnant. Then ask the pituitary: if it is pouring out FSH, the ovary is not answering; if FSH is low, the brain is not sending the signal. Age decides whether a failing ovary is called premature ovarian insufficiency or menopause. Scientific terms: secondary amenorrhea, hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis, negative feedback, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), estradiol, prolactin, TSH, progestin (progesterone withdrawal) challenge, premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
explanation.why: Estradiol and progesterone normally hold FSH down by negative feedback. When the ovary fails, feedback is lost and FSH rises; when the hypothalamus or pituitary fails, FSH is low or normal and estradiol is low. Pregnancy is excluded first in every patient.
explanation.measure: hCG (serum or urine) in every patient. First round: FSH (with LH and estradiol), prolactin, TSH; one review adds testosterone and pelvic ultrasound; androgen panel if hyperandrogenism. Progestin challenge (older step): medroxyprogesterone acetate 5–10 mg for 5–10 days, bleeding 2–7 days after = positive; experts caution routine use because it may be unreliable. POI (ESHRE 2024): age <40, ≥4 months amenorrhea or irregular cycles, FSH >25 IU/L once (repeat after 4–6 weeks if uncertain). Natural menopause (WHO): 12 consecutive months without menstruation with no other cause, generally age 45–55. FSH in mIU/mL equals IU/L.
explanation.differs: High FSH + low estradiol (ovarian failure: POI if <40, menopause at the usual age) vs low/normal FSH + low estradiol (central, such as functional hypothalamic amenorrhea) vs FSH that is not high (high prolactin, PCOS, uterine causes such as Asherman syndrome).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the first test in amenorrhea (hCG), interpret high FSH with low estradiol by age, recognise low FSH with low estradiol as central, and spot the claim that a withdrawal bleed proves normal ovarian function.

comparisons.title: POI vs natural menopause
comparisons.distinguisher: Age and duration; both show high FSH with ovarian failure.

comparisons.title: Ovarian vs central amenorrhea

right.label: Central (hypothalamic/pituitary)
points: FSH and LH low or normal

comparisons.distinguisher: FSH level: lost feedback raises it; a silent pituitary does not.

mnemonic.text: Rule out the baby, then ask who is shouting: a pituitary shouting high FSH at a silent ovary means ovarian failure; a whispering pituitary means the problem is upstream.
mnemonic.explanation: Puts hCG first and uses FSH to locate the lesion.
mnemonic.limitation: Hormonal contraception can lower FSH; high prolactin, PCOS and uterine causes do not raise FSH; an uncertain FSH may need repeating; the analogy ignores LH and age.

analogyLimitations: The shouting/whispering picture simplifies hormone feedback.
takeaway: Rule out pregnancy first, then read FSH alongside prolactin and TSH, because a high FSH points to ovarian failure, which is premature ovarian insufficiency before age 40 and menopause after twelve months without periods at the usual age.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old has had no menstrual period for 5 months. She says she is not sexually active. What is the first laboratory test?

options.rationale: Correct. Pregnancy is excluded first in every patient, regardless of the stated sexual history.
Incorrect. It is not a first test, and experts caution against routine use because it may be unreliable.
Incorrect. FSH belongs in the first round, but pregnancy is the first thing to exclude, and FSH alone would miss prolactin and TSH.
Incorrect. AMH is not a primary diagnostic test; it may help confirm POI when FSH is inconclusive.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old not using hormonal therapy has had amenorrhea for 6 months. hCG is negative, prolactin and TSH are normal, FSH is 62 IU/L and estradiol is low. Best interpretation?

options.rationale: Correct. Under 40, at least 4 months of amenorrhea and FSH >25 IU/L meet the ESHRE 2024 criteria; low estradiol supports it.
Incorrect. Ovarian failure before 40 is called POI; natural menopause usually occurs between 45 and 55.
Incorrect. That is a central cause with low FSH and LH, not high FSH.
Incorrect. Prolactin is normal, and a central cause would not raise FSH.

questions.stem: Which statement about the progestin (progesterone withdrawal) challenge is best supported by current reviews?

options.text: It may be unreliable, and a withdrawal bleed does not exclude ovarian insufficiency
options.rationale: Correct. Experts caution routine use because it may be unreliable and gives false-negative withdrawals, and a published woman with POI bled after it.

options.text: It must be completed before FSH can be measured
options.rationale: Incorrect. Current reviews measure FSH with prolactin and TSH in the first round after hCG.

options.text: No bleeding proves an outflow tract obstruction
options.rationale: Incorrect. No bleeding may also reflect low estrogen, and the test can give false-negative results.
Incorrect. Pregnancy is excluded with hCG before any hormone is given.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 26 Hit 5 and Exam Trap 3 present a fixed five-step order with FSH/LH only after a progestin challenge. Gibson 2020 and Nelson 2023 measure FSH (with LH/estradiol), prolactin and TSH together in the first round after hCG, and Gibson 2020 notes experts caution routine progestin challenge because it may be unreliable, with false-negative withdrawals (register flag rv-amenorrhea-fixed-sequence).

Ch. 26 Hit 14 labels 12 months amenorrhea + FSH 85 + estradiol <10 as “primary ovarian failure (menopause)” without age. Under 40 this is POI (ESHRE 2024, which needs only 4 months of disordered cycles); natural menopause is recognised after 12 months, usually at 45–55 (WHO) (register flag rv-fsh-menopause-vs-poi).
